analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 222 House cosponsors, a House majority, but never received a vote in committee or on the floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently repealed the federal estate tax, which taxes very large inheritances passed to heirs, and the generation-skipping transfer tax, which applies when wealth is passed directly to grandchildren. It would have kept a 35% gift tax with a $5 million lifetime exemption, so wealthy people could still give large sums during life at a rate lower than the 40% estate tax rate in effect that year [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and died there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. The estate tax only applies above a large exemption (a $5 million-per-person exemption indexed for inflation, with a 40% top rate in 2013), so repeal is worth the most to the roughly few-thousand wealthiest households each year whose estates are big enough to owe the tax. Families below that threshold already paid nothing.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the estate tax entirely for people dying after enactment, eliminating the tax on large inheritances passed at death [S2][S3].

It also repeals the generation-skipping transfer tax, which taxes very large transfers that bypass a child and go straight to grandchildren, a common technique in multigenerational trust planning [S2][S3].

It makes permanent a 35% gift tax rate with a $5 million lifetime exemption, adjusted for inflation, so the wealthy could continue moving assets to heirs during life at a lower rate than the 40% estate tax rate in effect in 2013 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The estate tax raises tens of billions of dollars a year almost entirely from multi-million-dollar estates; repealing it means either cuts elsewhere, larger deficits, or higher taxes on everyone else to make up the difference. Ordinary households currently owe no estate tax, so their only direct effect is through the lost revenue.

drawbacks.text: Repeal eliminates a tax that in 2013 fell only on estates above roughly $5 million per person ($10 million per couple), so the benefit concentrates in a tiny share of the wealthiest families while the federal government loses the revenue [S2][S3].

Keeping the gift tax at 35% with a $5 million lifetime exemption while repealing the estate tax creates a cheaper path for large wealth transfers during life than the tax applied at death that year, allowing the biggest fortunes to move money to heirs at a lower rate [S2][S3].
The bill contains no replacement revenue for the repealed taxes, so its full cost adds to the deficit unless offset elsewhere.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to a small group of the wealthiest households; a married couple could already pass about $10 million tax-free in 2013. The cost — the lost estate-tax revenue, on the order of tens of billions of dollars a year — is spread across all federal taxpayers. As drafted, the bill is a large tax cut for concentrated wealth with no offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never took it up and the full House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kevin Brady introduced the bill on June 19, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S1][S5].
It attracted 222 cosponsors — 218 Republicans and 4 Democrats — a numerical majority of the House [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the record: no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's failure is a win for ordinary federal taxpayers, who kept the estate tax that draws revenue almost entirely from multi-million-dollar estates. The largest estates and their heirs are better off that it never became law: the tax on their inheritances remained, and Congress's refusal to even schedule a vote kept repeal off the table for the 113th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest estates kept paying the tax

sides.party_line_note: The 222 cosponsors were 218 Republicans and 4 Democrats, so support was overwhelmingly but not entirely along party lines; the bill never advanced far enough to produce a roll-call vote.

industries.note: Repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes would eliminate a tax owed almost exclusively by multi-million-dollar estates, preserving more wealth for their heirs. The public's interest runs the other way because that revenue would otherwise come from those households rather than from everyone else.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers, trust administrators, and wealth managers
industries.note: Repealing the estate tax would shrink a professional industry built on structuring estates to avoid it, though the retained gift tax and $5 million lifetime exemption would keep some planning work in place.
